title: Beyond Flat Walks: Compositional Abstraction for Autoregressive Graph Generation
claim: Complex structures can be coarsened into communities and serialized hierarchically, with back-edges linking elements, yielding a compact token sequence.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, arrows between stages, boxed tokenization panel
description: A three-stage left-to-right pipeline illustrated on a molecule (camptothecin). The left panel, 'Input Molecule', shows a 3D ball-and-stick rendering with gray carbon, blue nitrogen and red oxygen atoms. An arrow leads to 'Community Coarsening', where the same molecule has teal and pink shaded regions for the two big communities (C7, C6). Six small gray-circled singleton atoms (C0–C5) are labeled, and dotted blue lines link the communities. A second arrow leads to a rounded blue-bordered box titled 'H graph tokenization'. It holds a tree with root R, singleton leaves, and C6 (red) and C7 (teal) nodes fanning out to child atoms. Orange back-edge arcs run beneath the leaves. A 'serialize' arrow points down to rows of dark tokens (SOS, ENTER, EXIT, EOS) with colored index tokens and bracketed orange back-edge tokens.
caption: Encoding pipeline, illustrated on camptothecin. Motif coarsening gives two nonsingleton communities (C6, C7) and six singleton communities (C0–C5), defining H. HDT serializes the hierarchy depth-first: [ENTER]/[EXIT] delimit communities, and back-edge brackets connect each atom to previously emitted neighbors within or across communities (orange arcs). The sequence is abridged, retains original atom indices, and omits atomand bond-type tokens.
abstract: Autoregressive graph generators typically linearize graphs through flat node-edge walks, which can obscure higher-order structure in large and complex graphs. We introduce a hierarchical graph abstraction and coarse-to-fine generation pipeline that separates coarsening, tokenization, and decoding. This exposes three design axes: community coarsening, hierarchical tokenization, and order randomization. Across these axes, traversal-based hierarchy consistently improves distributional and structural fidelity, while its V.U.N.\ cost depends strongly on the coarsening and randomization policy. In particular, the fidelity--V.U.N.\ trade-off observed under within-community randomization is substantially reduced when traversal order is randomized across the full hierarchy. With a fixed backbone, training protocol, and matched training time across five molecular and five non-molecular benchmarks, hierarchical serialization yields consistent distributional and structural gains on all molecular datasets, while the non-molecular results further show that these gains depend on how well the supplied hierarchy aligns with structure in the target distribution. Together, these results characterize when and how hierarchical serialization benefits autoregressive graph generation.
